utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good afternoon, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, I am on channel four, that I can see, and I'm receiving interpretation in French. Is it okay now? Yes. For the record, all the accused are present today. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Haynes. General, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back. At least from the information I have gathered, it doesn't seem likely that we will finish with you today, but we will still do our utmost. Mr. Vanderpuye, I take it that there are no preliminaries, correct? We hear none. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And before you continue, this is the schedule that I am suggesting. We'll have the break at 3.45 as usual, up to 4.10, that means 25 minutes. And then the second break, instead of at 5.45 as usual will be at 5.55, and we will resume at 6.25. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And good afternoon to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify something that I noticed on the record yesterday. In response to a question I put to you concerning your report where I asked you if you had prepared any report at least for the purposes of court, the record indicates that you said -- when I asked you if you had prepared any other report, in response to whether or not this was your first report you said: "Yes, this is my first encounter with any court or the judiciary system as such." And I just wanted to first confirm if that is accurate or there was an error in the transcription?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should just add from the point of view of drafting the report, because I appeared before this court, I was called as an expert witness in the Milovanovic et al case. I think that's what it's called or the so-called Kosovo group.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that clarification. Now, when we left off yesterday I asked you how long you had met with the Gvero team and you indicated that you had met with him for about an hour or two; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my estimate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And I take it that you met with the Miletic team prior to the preparation of your testimony here last week?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met with General Miletic's team when I arrived here in The Hague. I came with an associate from the team from Belgrade and cooperation went quite smoothly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And in advance of your testimony, how long did you meet with the Miletic Defence team, that is, when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to The Hague, we met on Saturday afternoon and Sunday afternoon. I can't remember the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And for how long, approximately, did you meet with them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember this correctly, on Saturday we spoke for about two or three hours, and a little less on Sunday, perhaps not even two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And from the time that you prepared the report until your testimony here in The Hague, did you ever inform the Miletic Defence team that you had consulted with various professionals concerning your conclusions or concerning the issues that are covered by your report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said yesterday is something that the Miletic Defence team knows. I was very precise when it came to my work. When I started drafting my report, when I submitted my report, well, in the course of the work on the report itself, I didn't meet any experts nor did I speak to them. So I didn't provide any explanations with this regard because I wanted the report to be based on a precise method, and it can be precise only if there is one author, if only one person works on it. My colleague General Djokic, who has appeared before this Court, is a neighbour of mine. We live very close to each other and we go to work together every day. I didn't give him the report either, and I didn't consult him with regard to drafting this report because I didn't want him to tamper with the methodology I was applying, and I think that I said something to that effect yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All I can tell as a man who appreciates precision in the way he speaks, your testimony repeatedly refer to interviews that you conducted, and I'm wondering whether or not we are talking about interviews in the sense of a purposeful or a guided inquiry, or we are talking about a chat over some coffee. So if you would, could you please tell us what it is you meant when you said that you met with or interviewed people in respect of the conclusions that you reached in this case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subject I was to deal with as an expert is very precise, very well defined. And with regard to that well-defined subject, and -- well, I spoke to no one about this matter. However, this subject involves a very precise military position, scientific positions. It involves various relevant experiences, and these are matters that we always discuss. It's a matter of the general culture of people who have the same or similar ranks. The report submitted was never the matter of investigation because I was never involved in investigative work. I was involved in drafting expert reports, and the report is an analytic one and contains all the other relevant elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So when you say you checked this figure, as we spoke about yesterday, with a large number of officers, that really had nothing to do with your report and it's not in reference to anything that was prepared in connection with your report; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I have understood you correctly. Which numbers are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm referring to page 88 of your report, and I'm referring to page 29992 of your testimony upon questioning by my learned friend. We spoke about this briefly yesterday, and there was some confusion as to whether or not I was referring to the term "diagram," as is written in the transcript, or whether or not we were referring to a figure. In either event, in the context of your testimony, you said that you had checked this with a large number of officers engaged in organisational work. And my inquiry, my question is, if you didn't speak to anybody in connection with the preparation of your report or about your report, then what -- what figure is it that you are saying that you checked with all these people about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, you mentioned the number 88. My report consists of 72 pages, the report that was printed out, and the part that was submitted here, because some of it was abbreviated, that version consists of 70 pages. Later on I understood that you were probably referring to figure 14, and that -- that's what you were asking me about. This is a figure that relates to rank and order. The figure on rank and order or on this method wasn't created and analysed with anyone else or by working with the other people. I told you about that, that the methodology for drawing conclusions on rank and order was the subject of discussion. And we discussed the matter, among other things, when the Serbian Atlantic Council -- or, rather, when the war school, the military school from the USA came to visit, we spoke about the subject of rank in order to put these people up in an appropriate way. So methodology is in a certain sense always the subject of discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want to belabour the point, but I think my question is pretty straightforward. On page 29992 of your testimony on 12 January, you say: "I contacted additional interviews" -- this is starting on 29991, line 17. "I contacted additional interviews with those officers who dealt with the organisation of the Army of Republika Srpska and established on the basis of all this the precise rank and order in the Army of Republika Srpska." Then you go on and you say at 2992: "Based on all this" -- this is at line two. "Based on all this I reached the conclusion presented here," which is presented in your report. "I have checked this diagram with a large number of officers," and it says "diagram" in the record just so you are clear. "I have checked this diagram with a large number of officers engaged in organisational work and they all agreed with every detail of this diagram." My question to you, sir, is: Having said that and now represented before this Tribunal that you never showed this to anybody, how can you reconcile those two statements?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's very easy. It's very clear. You've omitted to refer to something from the very beginning. I don't know why you are doing this. I've told you about the methodology, the criteria used. I spoke to everyone about these matters who was competent in the field. I've also said that I spoke to certain military representatives to see how they dealt with those ranks. So that had to do with the methodology I followed. I checked the methodology, but no one was presented with this figure. If it had been prepared, perhaps I would have presented it, but I kept introducing variations when it came to methodology so as to have a consistent expert report and so as not to deviate from the line that I was pursuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, as I understand it, and as is indicated in your report, the object of this report was to evaluate the role of General Miletic as he served in 1995 as the Chief of the Administration for Training and Operations in the VRS; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You read out the introductory part in my report, and there you have the subject of the report. So it's on page 5 and it starts with item 1, subject of the investigation, time, context, location, and it ends with the events at the time. So that's from the introduction. That was the purpose of my work and the subject is defined under item 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the subject, no. If you have the objective in mind, yes. The subject is defined in a particular way, in a separate way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So it was not your intention to evaluate the role that General Miletic played in his function as the Chief of Administration for Training and Operations in 1995. That wasn't the object of your report.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that. I even wrote that down. That was the task and the objective, but the subject of my report is precisely defined under item 1, and it's called the subject -- or the conclusions, the findings. If you're referring to my objective, yes, that was my objective, and it was a task that I approached very seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You also attempted to evaluate his other duties that were beyond his post; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to find out whether he had any other duties that didn't fall under his work description.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In respect of evaluating these duties and his function as they actually occurred in 1995, did you speak to General Miletic at all concerning those matters?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Miletic expressed the desire to have me as an expert, and we then spoke about me accepting the task for drafting this expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you speak to him about his function as it was in 1995 while he was in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke about -- about the entire time-period that he spent in that position in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that you may have spoken to him about the time-period. I want to know whether or not you spoke to him about his function during that time-period.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We spoke about all the duties that he performed in the VRS, in the Republika Srpska Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When did you speak to him about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for certain, but it was about ten or 20 days before a proposal was made to have me engaged as a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how long would you say you spoke to him for about this particular subject matter?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I wouldn't like to give you an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you approximate? Was it 15 minutes or was it 5 hours?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would see each other for other reasons, too. I was also invited to the General's daughter's wedding. We would also meet each other together with other friends. He's the friend of some of my friends. If I gave you such an estimate, well, that wouldn't be serious. So I stand by what I said. I can't say how much time the two of us allocated to the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were invited to his daughter's wedding; right? I just want to make sure the transcript is right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you have any personal friendship with General Miletic or his family?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the term "friendship" means different things in different cultures. However, if you have had a look at my CV, and I believe you have done so, you will have noticed that General Miletic and myself are of more or less -- come from more or less the same generation. We are both officers from the anti-aircraft missile units. We were both very successful officers. We knew each other, and I believe that we knew each other professionally and we were also on friendly terms. And our families didn't know each other, and the invitation to his daughter's wedding was a particular honour for me. It's not just an invitation that is extended to special friends. Such invitations also extended to acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. General --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How did it come to be that you were invited to General Miletic's daughter's wedding?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the reasons for which I was invited, well, you would have to ask General Miletic. I was very happy to receive that invitation and it was an honour for me to receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When did you receive it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is when I received the invitation?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the date. It was certainly before the wedding.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would imagine so. What year?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The years fly by, but I believe that General Miletic's daughter got married in 2006. I believe that that is what she herself told you here before the Tribunal. I'm not sure whether you're trying to check my recollection, but, yes, I was at the wedding.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you have you maintained contact with the Miletic family since then, between then and now?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "contact." I know, for example, that his daughter had professional contact with my wife. They worked for the same institution, and I went to express my condolences. Unfortunately, while General Miletic was detained here, a lot of unfortunate events that concerned his family. If this is the kind of contact that you are interested in, yes, I did have such contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you maintain any contact with General Miletic himself during this period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think my visit to General Miletic in the Detention Unit is on record, and I am not sure if he ever came over, but if I had the opportunity to do so I am quite sure that I greeted him and welcomed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure your visits are on record but I'm sure you wouldn't want the Trial Chamber and the Judges to go and have to look it up. So the reason why I am asking the question is so that you can put it on the record before these Judges so that they can evaluate what you have to say. Now, can you tell us how many times, for example, you visited General Miletic while he was here in custody?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the opportunity of visiting him twice, but given the bureaucracy in place, I visited him only once last January.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Last January, January of 2008; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, January of last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that in connection with the preparation of your report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a visit to a colleague. There's something I didn't want to comment on at all because I was present here when your expert presented the conclusions he arrived at in the report, and I didn't want to influence anyone as a result of my positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that a no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are asking me about the report, the answer is no. Although I knew that very soon thereafter I would be writing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you spoke to General Miletic about his service during the war, I take it you spoke to him within the framework of the topics that are covered by your report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not discuss the framework or the phases of my expert report. I said that I would define the topic of the expert report myself, and based on that I would draft my expert report. I did not want anybody influencing me in that respect. I did not want anybody to tamper with the definition of the subject of my expert report because I would not be able to proceed from such a definition. I would not be able to do my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, your report doesn't mention anything about having spoken to General Miletic about his duties at all, does it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that yesterday I said that no single conversation with anybody is mentioned because no conversation makes part of this expert report, and since no conversations make part of this expert report, then I don't have the right to refer to any such conversations. If I had quoted any of the conversations, then I would incorporate that into my methodology. I would do it in the way one does when writing an expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Page 29954 of the transcript, my colleague Ms. Fauveau put the following question to you: "Q. Could you tell us the sources you used to draft this report?" "A. I've used a number of sources. My main source was the source that I received from you, from the Defence. I also used materials that determined the position and the role of the organ that General Miletic worked for. I also used documents of the Yugoslavia People's Army, as well as the documents of the Army of Yugoslavia. I also used the search engines on the internet, and I compared the army with other modern armies such as NATO. I also used interviews with my colleagues because my colleagues, be it from the Army of Yugoslavia or the Army of Republika Srpska or even the militaries of the former Yugoslavia People's Army, I interviewed high-ranking officers from all these militaries." You identified that as the source of information that you used to draft your report. Did you use information that you derived from your conversations with General Miletic to draft your report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to make a distinction between two things here. I believe that we have been running in circles for too long now. However, this is your cross-examination so I don't mind repeating things for you. When you talk to anybody, when you have conversations with anybody, two processes are involved. One is the coordination of viewpoints, methodologies, the available knowledge, and other things; and the second process is the one aimed at establishing facts which will then be incorporated into your report. When it comes to establishing facts and the procedure that leads to it during conversations is very precise and very clear. This is called an interview. You define questions, you define answers you are aiming for, and then you state in the footnotes who you talked to and what the conversation was about. I did not use the second method, the latter method. I used the former method. However, I used it to a maximum potential and as much as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, is that a yes or a no to my question?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is part of a statement, and I can't say either yes or no. There are parts of your questions to which I can say yes and some other parts to which I could also say no. I believe that I have provided a very clear and precise answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My question, General, and I'll repeat it, did you use information that you derived from your conversations with General Miletic to draft your report, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the information that you used from General Miletic to draft your report, did you make counsel for the Defence, that is his Defence lawyers, aware of that information?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever I asked General Miletic and whatever he told me in answer to my questions, I subsequently received in the form of material that the Defence Counsel had available to them, and that's why the questions and answers did not mean much to me after that. Amongst other things, I asked him about his former duties. I didn't know that I would receive the complete personal history listing every position and the period of time. I was surprised to see such a precision and detail in all that. As for any other information that was not submitted to me by the Defence Counsel or that I got hold of -- hold of by reading books, for example, books that had been published, victors [as interpreted], as it were, no other piece of information provided to me verbally was used by myself in drafting my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of the information that you did use, as you've indicated you have, you didn't cite that in your report; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not everything. I read hundreds of reports. To be modest, I read hundreds of expert reports, conversations, interviews, books which are in the Prosecutor's collection, and similar things. In my report I was very precise. If I provided a statement, I tied that statement to a source, and in my expert report you have 142 footnotes which describe the sources that I used. And out of the 142 footnotes, some 17 per cent are relative to the BiH army; 69 per cent of the footnotes are relative to the documents originating from the Army of Republika Srpska -- I apologise, 48 per cent. 26 per cent is other types of literature and so on and so forth. This is only one part of the documents that I used. I did not incorporate everything because it would have been an impossible thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, don't you think that in preparing an analytical technical report such as this, even though it's your first one, that it would be appropriate to mention in the report itself that you spoke to the person who is the subject of the report and used information from that person in drafting it? Don't you think that would be an appropriate thing to do as a professional, as an expert such as yourself?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this would be necessary. What matters is that all the statements that I put in my report have been tied to the source, and this all has to do with a professional basis that I used in my capacity as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you speak to General Miletic about the nature of his defence to the charges in this case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The nature of General Miletic's Defence in respect of the charges is a matter for the Defence team. I did not want to discuss that with him. I only indicated to the team what road I would take as an expert. I already said at the outset that I am not an expert for the Defence. I am a military expert that was engaged by the Defence team to provide some facts. A military expert does not get involved in the nature of defence. A military expert deals with the essence of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With all due respect, General, you are also a military expert who happens to be a friend of an accused charged with a very serious crime and who happened to be invited to and, in fact, attended the wedding of the same accused. So my question to you is: Did you speak to General Miletic about his defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was absolutely precise, exceptionally precise, and there is no need for me to repeat. If there is need to do so, however, I can repeat whatever I have said so far. Friendship is no hindrance to an expert report. In my view, a hindrance to an expert report would be if you were a participant in the events that the accused has been charged with, and I can see that very often both direct and indirect participants in the events have been given a task to draft an expert report. I was not involved. I have all the competencies to draft such an expert report, and my personal friendships with people don't really play a role in this case. Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'll let the Trial Chamber worry about that. Now, you were asked some very specific questions concerning Directive number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that's 65 ter P5. If I could have that in e-court, please. If we could go to page 10 in the English or -- in the English, I believe. I am mistaken. It's page 10 in the B/C/S, and I believe it's page 14 in the English. And we should be looking at 6.1. Thank you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just before I get to this, I just want to ask you: When you spoke to General Miletic, did you take notes, perhaps, of your conversations that you had concerning what you ultimately used to draft your report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that I did not use anything in drafting my report. I did not use this method. I did not make any notes for that reason, and here I have some notes that I made in January last year during your expert's report or during your expert's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I know we have gone over this a hundred times, but I asked you specifically whether you used information that was provided to you by General Miletic in your report, and the transcript says that you said yes. And now you seem to be saying the exact opposite again.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think when I was examined by the Defence one of the first questions they put to me was about the sources, and when I listed my sources, I never said that -- the thing that you have just put to me. If you read my words carefully about the method of my work, I never mentioned and you will never find anywhere that I used as part of my method something that General Miletic provided to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, maybe I can help you find it, and you will find it on page 15 of today's transcript, lines -- page 14 of today's transcript, lines 11 through 14: "Q. My question, General, and I'll repeat it, did you use information that you derived from your conversations with General Miletic to draft your report, yes or no?" "A. Yes." There is no confusion about that, is there, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will have to provide a somewhat lengthier answer here at this point because this statement and this play-on words represents -- this game on words is quite a strong attack on my integrity, and I will be very precise here. I have been trying very hard at every moment to provide very correct, precise and concise answers in keeping with your request. So far for the gentleman, I made a distinction between the drafting of the report and consultations. One has to do with establishing facts, situations and methodologies or any such thing; and the second one is information. If you are trying to play games with these words when you put all that in the context of the question whether I informed the Defence Counsel for General Miletic about all that, I said that I checked all the information that I had received, that I was surprised when I saw how precise the material was and that I used the written material from the personnel file number 2. Any other attempt to take words out of the context is the reversal of the things that I said. I never used any facts or information that was provided to me verbally because if I had I would have used the methodology appropriate for entering such facts into a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You didn't take any notes. You didn't use any notes of any information that was provided by you -- provided to you by General Miletic; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not use any notes that I might have made in my conversation with General Miletic, and General Miletic did not provide me with any of his notes, either. No notes involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm curious because I've noticed that throughout your entire testimony you've been taking notes even though there is a reporter here and a transcript in front of you. Did you take any notes with respect to any of these interviews or any other information that you used in preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am forced to make notes for several reasons. Unlike you, an expert has his hands and legs tied. He does not have access to a database. He can't use his computer. He cannot go back to check. The only thing I can consult is what you provide me with. Very often the questions that are put here are too wide-ranging, they contain several sub-questions, and they use some methodologies that I am not familiar with, and in order to provide any answers I have to make notes. It is with great pleasure that I can provide my notebook to -- both to you and the Trial Chamber and you can inspect my notes. The transcript in front of me is of no use to me because I don't read English. My knowledge of English is very passive, and I am using the transcript in order to start my answer on time so as not to be admonished by the Trial Chamber that I am too fast in providing my answers. This is about the transcript. When it comes to the drafting of my expert report, I drafted one variation with over 300 pages. I have hundreds of notes on the computer. I am very good at using the computer. I have tables in Excel and some other documents which I can search, and this is what I do. And this is an integral part of a serious work, and I must tell you that I have been involved in a lot of serious work of this kind so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you asked for any of these things by the Defence for General Miletic, any of your notes or interviews or notes of interviews?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It never occurred to them or at least they did not tell me that. The General Miletic Defence did consult me on some professional issues. They wanted to hear my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you have those notes then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at this moment. The notes are on my computer in my apartment, and they were the basis of my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. What I mean is that you've retained them. That is, any notes that you've had, any interviews that you have conducted in preparing your report, you've retained; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a vast database which contains some book which I found in an electronic form. So this is a huge database that I can search. It is fully searchable, because that's how it was compiled. And anybody who needs anything from that database from me, I can certainly provide them with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Aside from the database, I am talking about notes now. Did you retain those?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "database" I imply documents that I have been provided with in any form, notes that I have made, books that I downloaded, and all the things that I have used in my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for clarifying that, General. We were looking at 65 ter P5, 6.1. Now, you were asked a series of questions concerning that. In particular, on paragraph -- I should say, rather, paragraph 122 of your expert you stated that: "This language does not fall within the scope of work of the operations and training organ with regard to formulating certain items of the directive." You also said that: "Neither the Operations and Training Administration nor its chief, General Radivoje Miletic, could have drawn up or modified item 6.1 of the directive." That's correct, isn't it? Let me just qualify that that's your conclusion; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was something else about this conclusion. There is another very important statement there. When Mr. Gvero's Defence asked me questions about this point, we agreed on the fact that the support to combat activities in 6.1 and then morale and psychological support, and there is no 6.2 or 6.3 or any similar thing, that that very fact points to the lack of professionalism in the drafting -- or, rather, non-military way of drafting this directive. So the first part is not an activity that the Administration for Operations and Training would be involved in, although they were the ones charged with the drafting of this document. It seems to me that the methodology that was used in this point is not something that would have originated from the Administration for Operations and Training.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, what you've said in regard to the quality of the language that is used, the methodology, that you said it's not military or I think you used the term "unsoldierly" previously, that's not something that is actually contained in your report, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This has not been provided in detail in my report because I did not deal with anything that was not part of the duties of the Administration for Operations and Training. As far as the sentence is concerned, yes, I did say that this was structured in a non-military or unsoldierly way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, you know that the directive itself indicates that General Miletic was its drafter; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. I've already said several times that the Main Staff of the Army Republika Srpska proposed an outline of the directive, not the directive itself, and that proposal went to there, and in that part of the work of the General Staff the job of General Miletic is not in dispute at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could just go to page 15 of the English and page 21 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, all I'm referring to is what it says where it indicates "drafted by," and it says "Colonel Radivoje Miletic." You see that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What point of my expert report is that? I can't go by pages. Can you direct me to the point in my expert report?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am asking you only this, only this: The document that's before you indicates that it is drafted by Colonel Radivoje Miletic. You see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this document, yes. What it says here shows that the proposal made in the document was made by Colonel Radivoje Miletic. The draft proposal was made by him. You have to make a distinction between the draft document and the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You refer in your report to a Directive number 7. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the documents you referred to in conducting your analysis is this document that's now before you; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so when I say to you that this document indicates that it's drafted by General Miletic, do you take issue with that as a matter of fact?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's absolutely problematic, and I think you understand what I am talking about here, but you're trying to confuse two issues, two theses here. The document drafted by Colonel Radivoje Miletic as a proposal was forwarded to the president of Republika Srpska, to the supreme commander, in other words. When this document was forwarded -- after it had been forwarded, I don't know what was done with it, but this is the final document that was created over there. On the basis of everything that has been analysed, I presented you with arguments and conclusions according to which it was highly probable that this document isn't identical with the draft document or, rather, the proposal that was sent to the president. I was quite precise about that both in my report and in the testimony that I gave last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. When you were determining whether or not the language that's contained in point 6.1 could be attributed to General Miletic, you did not put in your report the fact that it may be unsoldierly or unprofessional or sloppy as a possible basis; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a very precise reason. Point 6.1 is not a field of activity that the chief of the Administration for Operations and Training deals with, and I was quite precise about this. This document here was collectively drafted, and point 6.1 was not the subject of my expert report. Together with colleagues here we came to the conclusion that you yourself stated. The fact that it wasn't a subject of the report doesn't reduce the importance of the expert report which focused on other aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So the conclusion that you drew that it is unsoldierly and unprofessional was something that you drew during the course of your testimony. It wasn't some conclusion that you drew beforehand; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I had already reached that conclusion, but not on the basis of point 6.1 but on the basis of other points.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So you reached the conclusion in advance of drafting the report, but you never put it in the report per se; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things in point 3.34, I dealt with the distinction between the draft directive and the final directive. I dealt with the matter in detail, and I addressed the matter that you have asked me about. On that occasion and with regard to what you have referred to, well, it's an issue I addressed in one of the points that the Defence team for General Gvero also asked me about. For example, point 1.39, we talked about an illogical task. In 1.40 we talked about the fact that it wasn't possible to have such task, and I think there is one point where I said that it -- I said quite precisely that, among other things, this wasn't a military task. It appeared to be an illogical task and it was for another organ to deal with. As for the shortcomings of the directive in relation to the Operations and Training Administrative Unit, well, I was quite precise. I didn't analyse all the details, but I think that on the whole I have rounded things off quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go back to 10 -- page 10, I'm sorry, in the English, and page 14 in the B/C/S. Sorry, it's 10 in the B/C/S -- nope, 19 in the B/C/S, I think is what it was, and I think it was 14 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. General, with respect to this particular section, 6.1, you indicated when you were examined by Mr. Krgovic that -- well, he put the question to you, and this is at page 30244, lines 13 through 22 of the transcript: "Q. If you analyse the portion right here, you can see these elements being introduced, such as logistics, PVO support, things to do with mobilisation. This entire paragraph does not contain anything, at least in my view, that corresponds with morale and psychological support. Not something that would seem to be in keeping with the rules of the military profession; right?" And your answer was: "Not only does it not correspond with this element of support for combat operation, this entire paragraph is not in keeping with its purpose. This entire paragraph that relates to support for combat operations and then with a specific emphasis on 6.1." You remember giving that testimony, giving that answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the next-to-last paragraph in the English --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- and I think we have to go to next page for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can see -- let me know if you can't, but I'll read it in English anyway. The next-to-last paragraph on the page in front of you says: "In the implementation" --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It should be page 21 of the B/C/S. I can't tell if that's what's in front of us. All right. I think it is the next-to-last paragraph before number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: "In the implementation of other forms of support for combat operations, all measures are to be taken according to Directive number 6. The focus of logistic support in 1995 shall be on units envisaged for the execution of strategic level operations." You see that; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you know that Directive number 6 provides for combat support in terms of morale and psychological support, intelligence support, security support, engineering support, anti-nuclear chemical and biological support, counter-electronic support, and logistics support. You know that; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am fully aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So it's not anomalous or unusual that those particular categories are not listed under this section individually since it's referred to or incorporated by reference?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is unusual and methodologically unjustified. Directive number 6 has quite opposite purposes. It was issued about 15 or 16 months prior to this one. If I am not mistaken, Directive number 6 dates back to November 1993; whereas, this directive dates back to March 1995. Not a single soldier would rely on that directive because I see here that an attempt is being made to accept item 6. I'd like to emphasize a fact that is quite noticeable at this point in time and that is that the paragraph between the one that you read out and the previous one, well, these paragraphs are far removed from other paragraphs. It shows that someone tampered with the digital text. One can't refer to support for combat operations from the previous period, and it's also not justified in methodological terms. You can see that something very unusual has been done here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You don't have any personal information that anybody tampered with the electronic version of this instrument, do you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would mean that I was a participant in the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't know if there is a translation error, but it might mean -- well, let me re-ask the question. You don't have any information that this particular document in its electronic form was tampered with in any way; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such information, but on the basis of the facts I can reach a given conclusion. To help you understand the matter, I would like to point something else out. When you try -- when we try to move support for combat operations under 6 to support for combat operations under 7, if you bear in mind the characteristics of what is written under 6 and the Directive 7, it says that the matters are defensive, well, things are quite clear because support for combat operations at the time cannot be taken -- or, rather, adopted from that directive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we have the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will resume at 10 minutes past 4.00 exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When we left off, I asked you if you had any personal information that anybody had tampered with the electronic version of this Directive 7, and you indicated that you had no such information. Did you ask General Miletic about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could take a look at 6.1 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in the middle of the second paragraph -- or third paragraph, I'm sorry, it reads -- well, let me read the whole paragraph or a part of the beginning: "Externally, a more aggressive propaganda and information presence should be maintained aimed at gaining allies, deepening discord in the coalition, unmasking the biased and hostile activities of certain individuals and parts of UNPROFOR and some humanitarian organisations and undermining the enemy's fighting morale. This is to be achieved through planned and organised information and propaganda activities coordinated from state level." Now, having read that and having reviewed that, this is clearly something that would be attributed to the administration for legal -- well, morale, legal, and religious affairs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And this is what I said last time. First of all, we have to bear in mind the fact that Directive number 7 was issued at the state level or the national level, as you can see in the figure, and this text is intended for someone who works with the government. It's intended for ministries and other organisations. The administration for morale, religious, and legal affairs doesn't deal with such organisations. And although I am not an expert on morale, they would never apply such a text, use such a text, because these groups are not their target groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's continue. It further reads that this is to be achieved through the planned and organised information and propaganda activities coordinated from the state level and says: "Internally, raise the awareness of people and soldiers of the necessity and possibility of waging an armed struggle and militarily defeating the enemy. Make them so aware of the need -- make them also aware of the need to put all available human and material resources at the disposal of the liberation struggle in order to create a free and unified Serbian state in the former Yugoslavia." Now, in your view, is this language consistent with the function of the Administration for Morale, Religious, and Legal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something has been mixed up here. There are some sentences that might be sentences used by this department, but most of the sentences are sentences that would be attributed to the commander and government or the government of Republika Srpska. It's language that would be used by those bodies. I'd emphasize the items that have to do with raising the level of awareness of the people. This is the state's responsibility. Then it says, Place all personnel and material resources at the disposal of the liberation fight, and the Supreme Command and the president deal with such matters. Together with the Supreme Command, these elements that have to be used in combat. So it's not something that falls under the competence of this department, and you can see that this language is intended for elements from that system.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 3029, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, General, I take it you've seen this document before; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps. I am not sure, but perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a decision for further operations. It is dated 24th November 1992. It was issued on the heels of Directive 4 of 19 November 1992, and it's signed by Commander Colonel Milenko Zivanovic. Paragraph 1 of this document, you can see that it refers essentially to Directive number 4. It's 023 of 19 November 1992, and it reads: "I have decided launch an attack using the main body of troops and major equipment to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up or force them to surrender, and force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde." You see that; right? What I am interested at this point is, rather, section 2.3(c) which will be on page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it. It's item 1 in the decision, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right. Now, I am going to refer you to item 2.3(c) which is page 2 in the English and it's page -- should be page 3 in B/C/S. Now, I am only going to refer you to the section that concerns moral, psychological preparations, and the language of that section reads as follows: "Before initiating any kind of operation, inform the unit members about the important aim of that operation and underline that the outcome of minor actions and of the whole operation is of crucial importance to the realisation of the aim of the Serbian people, namely, the creation and establishment of a Serbian state in these areas." Now, that language is consistent with the language that you see in Directive 7, 6.1, particularly concerning informing soldiers of the liberation struggle in order to create a free and unified Serbian state; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to provide you with a detailed explanation. You know as well as I do that I am a military expert whose field relates to organisation, management, and command. If we are now dealing with morale and psychological preparations and security, well, I am not specifically competent for that. I can talk about it in technical terms, but in terms of methodology it wouldn't be appropriate or it's highly inappropriate for you to put questions to me that are based on an order that relies on Directive 6, and you are asking me to compare it to Directive 7. In methodological terms this is quite inappropriate, but if you are trying to establish some kind of a link, it is necessary to do so by referring to this point -- or, rather, the entire point. This order is based on Directive 6, and then you might try to see whether morale and psychological preparations correspond to Directive 6, or perhaps 4. If it's November 1993, I think the directive concerned is Directive 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if I have understood the answer, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I haven't understood it. If I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you could clarify it with the witness, please. Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This document, sir, is a decision for further operations issued by the Drina Corps command. It is signed by Milenko Zivanovic as commander. It is a military document, and it indicates in its header --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- that it refers to -- it refers to a directive of the Main Staff of the Army Republika Srpska, strictly confidential, number 02 /3 of 19 November 1992. And paragraph 1 or item 1 refers to a decision of the commander, as you have been talking about. It is dated 24 November 1992. I think I may have mentioned. And let me point out that the section that I am referring to in particular, I do realise I did make an error. It is actually number 3(c). The indentation is kind of hard to see, but it's number 3, item 3. And item 3 reads: "Support" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we have to go to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ah, yes, next page in the English. I'm sorry, I didn't realise that we had moved. Okay. And if you could look at the top, maybe, of the B/C/S version, I think we might be able to see the title. No? It's on the previous page. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In any event, number 3, item 3 refers to support for -- support to combat operations, and item (c) is morale and psychological preparations. So my question is: In light of those facts, it is true, is it not, that the language that is used concerning morale and psychological preparations is consistent with the language that is used in Directive 7, item 6.1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the witness remove his headphones, assuming, as he's already said, he doesn't answer any English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There was a moment where I thought he did understand and he could follow, but if anyone so wishes we can ask him to leave the courtroom right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't -- Your Honour, whilst the answer to the question as first asked was, I would concede, not clear, the witness has said: "If we are now dealing with morale and psychological preparations and security, well, I am not specifically competent for that." The question he has just been asked clearly relates to something which he has conceded he is not an expert to deal with and answer. He said that; he shouldn't be asked about it again, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the -- do you wish to comment, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the question is a very simple one. I mean, the question basically is look at the two texts, do they tally, do they say the same thing. You don't need to be an expert to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, in which case he doesn't really need to ask the question. It's rhetorical in many ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, because he could -- he could actually say, No, they are not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So be it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, what you are being asked is a very simple question. You are being asked to look at the two texts and tell us whether, to you, they practically or essentially mean the same thing or they say the same thing or whether you think that they differ, the one from the other. First of all, do you have the two texts in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have both. I just have the order of the Drina Corps, point 3(c), as far as I can tell. And the other text from the Directive 7, I believe that I remember it well. I don't have to have it in front of me to compare it. What matters here is a statement of some essence, and that is the language extended to the brigade and the language extended to the state cannot be similar, let alone the same. And the spirit of that language can be recognized by the expert. In point (c), this language is of the kind that would be used to send a letter to a much lower level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The idea of motivating one's own's soldiers, troops to armed struggle on the basis of securing freedom and state sovereignty, as it were, is not an unheard of concept in relation to the function of the Administration for Morale, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your first question which contains a statement in it is something that I would like to refer to and say that the statement is not correct. Moral guidance is the duty of all the officers across the army and not only of one administration. The administration is only the professional body in that respect, a professional organ. So that idea, that concept is based primarily on the goals and the Administration for Moral Guidance is the one that operationalises the elements in a professional way. As for the credibility of that work and the competence of the Administration for Moral Guidance, I am really not the best suited person to talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, under who's competence would morale and psychological support or preparations be, given this full method of work that you have indicated was employed in drafting directives and, indeed, some orders? Who would contribute to that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The organs in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What organ would that be? What organ is in charge of developing or making submissions concerning morale and psychological support or preparations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level of the Main Staff it would be the sector for moral guidance, psychological, legal, and religious affairs. At the corps level, I believe it would be departments. And at the department level it would -- I apologise, at the division level it would be departments and sections. In the brigades I believe it would be departments and sections as well. I am not sure. I did not analyse that in detail, in depth. However, the professional and functional authority is established along the vertical line.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What organ would be responsible for making submissions concerning planned and organised information or propaganda within the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army Republika Srpska and almost all the militaries from the region did not have organs for information and propaganda, and especially not in peacetime. And this derived from the character of -- or the nature of the war from which they were being prepared. One could draw an analogy and say that something of that sort was needed. It would be the commanders who would give it to that organ to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could have 5D759, please, in e-court. And I believe I need page 18 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And for your reference, since you have it in front of you, General, I am referring to figure 3 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe we could blow that up just a little bit. It might be of some assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what we have in e-court now is a diagram -- or I should say a figure showing the organisational chart. On the far left --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand it's page 15 in B/C/S. In any event, the figure is in B/C/S as it's written.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On the far left we have the staff. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And next to that we have the sector for moral guidance, religious, and legal affairs; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Moral guidance, religious, and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we go down that organisational chart we will see that immediately beneath where you have indicated "sector," it says, "Department for moral guidance and religious affairs"; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Department for moral guidance and religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And beneath that you can see it says: "Information and PPD, political and propaganda activities department"; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Psychological -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And beneath that you have the civilian affairs department and then the legal affairs department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it is a fact, sir, that the moral guidance, religious, and legal affairs sector oversaw or -- rather, I should say, the information and political propaganda activities department fell underneath the sector for moral guidance and religious affairs -- religious and legal affairs; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you know, having reviewed the documents in this case or of many of the documents you were provided, that General Gvero was the head of the sector for moral guidance and religious affairs. He was the assistant commander for that organ in the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in 1995 you know that Savo Sokanovic was the chief of the department for moral guidance and religious affairs; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you know that Milovan Milutinovic was the head of the information, political and propaganda activities department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know these officers. I didn't know -- I did not research that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could may have 65 ter 6D284 in e-court, please. All right. If we could just go to the very last page of this document, it's ERN ending 76 in the B/C/S version so it should be the next page. And that would be page 4 in English. If I could, I just want to focus in on that stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have the original over here if you have trouble reading it, General. Are you able to make out what that stamp reads?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "Information Centre," I believe, if that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Are you able to read the circular part of the stamp?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, "Main Staff of the Army Republika Srpska," that's the first circle. "Sector for moral guidance, religious and legal affairs," is the second circle. In the inner most circle I believe it says "Centre," but it's not very legible, I'm afraid. If I were provided with the original, I might be able to do it a little better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps if we zoom out a little bit rather than zoom in. Not that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do happen to have the original if that will assist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. If you have the original that's easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could put that on the ELMO maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you able to read that, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Information Centre," that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir. And that document is dated 8 -- 22 of August, 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that would certainly indicate that that information, dissemination of information and propaganda would have fallen under the purview of the sector for moral guidance, religious and legal affairs. Wouldn't that indicate that to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One might conclude that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. Not yes, probably. Let me explain why such answer. Drawing conclusion on the activities of any single organisational units anywhere in the world, including this army here, based on a structural scheme where you can see a box and based on a stamp which shows that there was an information centre would be pure speculation, beyond one's authority. One would have to analyse all of their documents. I've already stated several times that the reconstruction of the organisational development of the armies on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina has never been carried out, and I could not derive any information about the existence of such a unit. I can say based on this that it probably did exist, that it probably had its own activity. So to be precise, the long and the short of it is probably that was the case, but I don't have any elements to draw a final conclusion on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, General. Let me take you to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter 4148, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: While that's loading up let me just ask you: Was it your understanding that one of the functions of the organ for moral guidance, religious and legal affairs, the sector as it existed in the Main Staff, one of its functions was actually to provide information and also propaganda; true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be precise, I can conclude that its activity was information, provide information and propaganda activity. When I say "information," I mean internal information of the troops which is an important activity, and I believe that propaganda activity also existed, but one would have to analyse that based on the activities that were actually carried out and on the powers that were regulated by a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, if you look at this document which is dated 13 April 1993, this follows the activity surrounding Directive 4, the Cerska campaign, Konjevic Polje, you can see that at the bottom, the last paragraph of this document -- it's a Drina Corps document for the record. It's directed to the Main Staff, moral, religious, and legal affairs section. In the last paragraph it reads: "In order to react in a correct and timely manner and take all the necessary measures, we ask for your engagement in this manner through the following: To engage your bodies in the resolution of the problem of the population that wants to leave Srebrenica, that assistant commander for morale, General Gvero, and his bodies should engage themselves with projecting information to the Muslims of Srebrenica on the means of their safe evacuation from the combat zone." That is precisely an appropriate application of the organ of moral guidance, religious and legal affairs; is it not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely incorrect. I am not an expert. You have to ask General Zivanovic that. In all the schools where I worked, where I studied this, and in practice wherever necessary, I requested assistance from this organ to be extended to my units, to my troops, not to the civilians. And I really don't know where this request on behalf of General Zivanovic came from. What he wanted, how he wanted it done, organs for moral guidance, religious, and legal affairs extend support to commands when it comes to the information, motivation, and mobilization of their own troops. And here one could conclude that General Zivanovic is privy to some information about the existence of some forces or means that may be engaged for this task, but I believe you will have to look for an answer to your question from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we wanted to let the witness finish, but again, now he has finished, perhaps he can take his headphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, General, please, if you could remove your headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, as it happens, he's given a rather favourable answer from our point of view, but we weren't to know that in any way. That's not really the point of this objection. Judging by the general tenor of the Prosecution cross-examination of this witness, they have approached him, at least to begin with, in the same way as the Gvero Defence did, namely to seek to undermine him partly in relation to his credibility and primarily so far as his expertise is concerned. Our cross-examination was directed at two areas; namely, Directive 7 and in particular his placement and ranking of our client within the VRS, in effect figure 14 of his report. Those assertions which undermined our case in part were challenged and we cross-examined him accordingly. Beyond those two areas, we did not advance anything with this witness. The Trial Chamber has really been here before. Our objection is that yet again the Prosecution are using a Miletic witness as a vehicle to further the case against our client. And we go one stage further. These questions are a calculated gamble on the part of Mr. McCloskey and his team to ask questions which they would otherwise have put to our expert. They, gambling that we are not in fact going to call him. Now, previously I have objected on the basis of saying where is this going. I think it was in relation to a cross-examination of Mr. Vanderpuye of another witness, and Mr. McCloskey got up, and I make no bones about that because no we -- no criticism of that, perhaps I should say, because Mr. Krgovic and I share matters in a similar way, and he said that he wasn't prepared for his advocates to reveal where they were going. We didn't pursue that, but we do suggest that this is going in an inappropriate direction. This is straying well beyond the subject matter, one, of the expertise of the witness; and two, of the matters in hand, but above all else, this is a clear attempt by the Prosecution to further the case against Gvero. One only needs to look at the list of documents they have supplied with a dozen new ERN numbers relating to Gvero to show and illustrate that particular point, and the Trial Chamber should put a stop to it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment -- thank you, Mr. Josse. Do you wish to comment, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I think some comment is necessary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, then, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First of all, as I indicated and I prefaced this entire line of cross-examination on reading back to the witness his statements in connection to a question that was put to him by Mr. Krgovic during his cross-examination, if you would like to call it that, of this witness, considering the fact that they proofed him and met with him for a substantial period of time prior to his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still a cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I know. In particular the question was, if you analyse this particular document, referring to Directive 7 and in specific reference to 6.1, Mr. Krgovic stated: "This entire paragraph does not contain anything, at least in my view, that corresponds with morale and psychological support." Which this witness has identified as falling relatively within the competence of the organ for which General Gvero was in charge in 1995. The witness responded saying, "Not only does this correspond -- not only does this not correspond with this element for support," meaning the element of psychological and morale support, "this entire paragraph is not in keeping with its purpose." This line of cross-examination continued for a substantial period of time during the cross-examination of this witness. Because the report itself suggests that that language could not have been written by the organ over which General Miletic was responsible, putting in parentheses morale and psychological support, that is the basis upon which my learned friends decided to cross-examine this witness because what's contained in the expert report suggests that the organ for which General Gvero is responsible may have contributed to the items that is being contested by the Miletic Defence in Directive 7, 6.1 in particular. We have introduced these documents to respond specifically to that issue because that issue concerns the role and responsibilities of General Gvero as the assistant commander for moral guidance, religious, and legal affairs, which is the subject -- which was specifically the subject of the cross-examination and is a relevant part of the expert report insofar as it relates to the attribution of General Miletic as the drafter of the entirety of that directive. And so it seems abundantly clear that anything having to do with what General Gvero's role was in respect of discharging his duties as they are articulated in Directive 7, that is information and propaganda, are directly responsive to the arguments that are raised by the Defence and are directly relevant to the material that is proffered in the expert report itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you wish to comment further Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, just this. Mr. Vanderpuye, we submit is conceding that he is opening up the ambit well beyond the scope of the cross-examination; but secondly, and more importantly than that, the cross-examination was responsive, as Mr. Vanderpuye has in effect just conceded, to what the expert just said in his report.
