In other words, a certain amount of it we really had to cross-examine upon. And in particular, so far as this gentleman is concerned, for Mr. Vanderpuye to throw in our face the fact that we had proofed him is rather unfair, very -- well, yes. I saw your reaction, Your Honour, because the witness is a problem to us. He doesn't help our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, you had every right to --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is simply indefensible to say that, Well, because we had to cross-examine him, we were put in a position where we had to open the door to introduce evidence that you have a right to cross-examine on. That's simply indefensible. It's a non sequitur and it makes no sense whatsoever legally or in any other sense. My colleague has articulated a position which, number one, is completely incorrect. I do not concede that they had to cross-examine this witness. I've been a Defence attorney for 13 years before I came here, and no, you did not have to cross-examine this witness even if the witness presents evidence that is troublesome to you. But the fact that you choose to cross-examine the witness -- and I have to admit I am somewhat surprised that my colleague is making this argument because he submitted a position with respect to the use of documents on this very issue that was supportive of the fact that you cross-examine at your own peril. And in this particular instance, this was an issue that was specifically targeted and raised by Mr. Krgovic. The words, "This entire paragraph does not contain anything, at least in my view, that would correspond with morale and psychological support ..." did not come from the witness. These were words that Mr. Krgovic spoke in guiding the witness to the answer that he wanted to get from him, and these documents, in our position, is directly and specifically responsive to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we have heard enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just this, Your Honour. Your Honours observed before that as far as Mr. Vanderpuye and I are concerned, we used the same language but with we come from different legal cultures. Rule 92, Rule 90(b) -- give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the counsel to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I will do, I apologise. Your Honour, Rule 90(h)(2), we say we are under a duty to put our case. I say it's a matter of legal culture because I know that American lawyers and English lawyers take a radically different approach to that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are all agreed here. We come to the conclusion, Mr. Josse and Mr. Vanderpuye, that the line of questions that have been put so far on this issue by Mr. Vanderpuye arise out of both the witness's report and part of the cross-examination of the Gvero Defence team of this witness. So we authorise the continuation of this line of questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- until we decide otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Nothing. May I continue, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think you have the transcript of what I said that means that you are authorised to continue unless we stop you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Headphones again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think you just indicated that you didn't believe that this fell within the competence -- that what is being requested within this document, did not fall within the competence of the organ for morale, religious, and legal affairs; is that right? That is, in your expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to the information I had, that was the case because the activities of those bodies were mainly focused on the internal organisation of the Army of Republika Srpska and of the other armies that were created subsequent to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so it wouldn't be appropriate for someone like -- or someone in General Gvero's position or General Gvero himself to have direct contact, for example, with international organisations concerning the Srebrenica situation in 1995, would it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for whether it was appropriate for him to have contact with international organisations, well, I can't link that up to these requests because in the request mention is made to offensive and informative work that is supposed to have other consequences. So I can't establish a link between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you know that this particular request followed the campaign that occurred on the heels of Directive 4; right? You can tell that just by looking at the date, can't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to the date it's the period after the Directive number 4 and prior to Directive number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 4201 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have it on the monitor, please? Could the Registrar be of assistance?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As you can -- well, this document is not translated, but I will read to you what it says. It's dated 23rd May 1993. It's entitled "Conflict in the Balkans: Exuding Confidence, Serbian Nationalists Act As if War for Bosnia is Won," and this is a New York Times article.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we turn to the last page of the article -- it's 3 pages it should be page 3. What's that? One page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me just put this to you and you can comment on it. The last paragraph of the document - we will find it and get it into e-court - reads: "Antipathy for Muslims" -- Well, it's the fourth from the bottom of that paragraph -- of the end of the article. "Antipathy for Muslims and hostility toward anybody suspected of having sympathy for them is widespread. Allied to the suspicion is a conviction belied by every fact of the war that Serbs have been its principle victims. On Monday, nationalist officials organised a trip to the village of Fakovici to what officials said had been a massacre of Serbian civilians by Muslims fighters. On arrival, reporters found forensic experts from the military hospital in Belgrade, the Serbian capital, at open air tables examining the remains of 20 Serbs said to have been killed on June 21, 1992. At least seven were males wearing military uniforms. Mosques reduced to rubble. "The event appeared to have been presented for political purposes. Grieving relatives said the bodies had been buried soon after the villagers were killed and then exhumed, exhibited to reporters, and reburied. The deputy commander of the Serbian nationalist forces, General Milan Gvero, presided. "Reporters driving to the event travelled 35 miles down the Drina Valley past houses that had been blasted by tank fire, mosques that had been reduced to rubble, and tractors blown up by the roadside. At every stop there was nothing but silence. But one point that Serbian officials were keen to make seemed uncontrovertible: That Serbs who lived in the valley are implacably opposed to living with Muslims again, much less to surrendering political control to Muslims as required by the peace plan. General Gvero put it bluntly. 'We say everybody has to live on his own territory: Muslims on Muslim territory, Serbs on Serbian,' he said, 'This is pure Serbian territory and no power on earth can make it surrender it.'" In the context of what we have been discussing, is what General Gvero is engaged in, that is meeting with reporters, making statements concerning the objectives or the purposes of the Serbian position, is that appropriate to his position as assistant commander for moral guidance and religious, and legal affairs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes -- are you ready? Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I repeat my objection. This is nothing but veiled -- or perhaps veiled is the wrong word. This is nothing but prejudice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any remarks?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes -- THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise for getting to the feet in the course of these proceedings, however, there is one thing that I was particularly affected by in addition to all the other fabrications. There is a reporter here, but we don't have a text. We don't have evidence according to which this was written somewhere, but this text says that Gvero presided over a funeral. I don't know what that means in any civilized country. General Gvero was at the funeral of these people who had been killed, and as far as I can remember, he said a few appropriate things. Never would it be possible for anyone to prove that Muslims had to live apart from the Serbs and on different land. That's a pure lie. Is there a single piece of evidence from the Prosecution according to which someone else said that when loads of journalists were present? This witness is a witness for organisation and establishment, an expert for that subject, but the Prosecution has been insisting on having the witness address subtle and professional issues of morale and intelligence. On five occasions he said that he competent for that field. With all due respect for the Tribunal, for the Prosecution, I think that this idea that the witness isn't competent to address the issue is something that should be taken into account because this is something that he has stated. And I say this with all due respect for the Tribunal. Once again, I am very sorry for having felt the need to get to my feet, but I was seriously affected by this fabrication of a journalist that hasn't been supported by any documents. He has written about things that he probably hadn't experienced himself. I thank you very much and I do apologise once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. For the future I would suggest that when you have something like this on your mind, that you ask to contact your Defence team who are here precisely to represent you and also your complaints when they exist, and I am sure that they are best placed and qualified to present them to the Tribunal, perhaps, in a better way than you can, and also decide what should be said and what should better not be said at all. So any time you need to consult with your lawyers, please draw your attention and we will give you every opportunity. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a particular difficulty here because I am told by Mr. Krgovic that we think that this document has only just been released into e-court. It's certainly in English, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's not been translated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- and indeed it wasn't on the screen. I've managed to get it up on my screen, but I have access to different material than my client. And that's fully compounded the problem. That was apparent to me in translation from what my client was saying. I don't know whether he would like a few minutes with his Counsel, whether that would help matters or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what I am suggesting. I come from a jurisdiction when normally we would advise the accused to be parsimonious with his words and have consultation with Counsel, because we believe that Counsel can present the case better.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't want to be -- upset General Gvero at all, but that's certainly the view of Mr. Krgovic and I. Although, to be fair to General Gvero, I know that there is a prevailing view in some of the Trial Chambers of this particular Tribunal that the accused should be able to chip in every now and then as they please. But if he'd like to speak to us, we would be more than happy to have a moment with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think my colleagues would agree to allow the possibility to consultation between General Gvero and his counsel and that can take place, if you wish to speak to your lawyers, but I understand even his lawyers wish to speak to him. If I --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Krgovic can go and speak to him there for a moment. Can I suggest that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even if they want to speak in one of the rooms outside, I mean, I have no objection to that. THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. President, thank you for the useful advice you have given me. I have tried to follow your advice at all times, but you yourselves have seen, and I don't know whose fault it is, but in this courtroom we have certain difficulties. I am in one corner and my Counsel in another. When I have the opportunity of consulting my counsel, well, it's already too late. So I would like you to bear this in mind. It's not necessary now for us to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand -- thank you for that, and I understand we can now proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. And, General Gvero, I do appreciate that there is a problem. The way -- the layout of the courtroom and the distance between accused and counsel is problematic, and it is more problematic in a case like this where we have seven accused and seven Defence teams. However, all you have to do - and this applies to each one of you - is to stand up and draw our attention, and we will give you every opportunity to discuss or consult with your Counsel. THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I hope we are nearing the end and that it won't be necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, have we sorted out? Because we haven't sorted out the matter raised by Mr. Josse. There were no remarks, but I need to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As I understand it, the objection has to do with the information or the reliability of the information that General Gvero raised: A, he hasn't had an opportunity to see the document; and B, he contests the veracity of the reporter. That's what I understand the issue to be. If it's a question of relevance, I think I can speak rather readily to that, clearly to it, but I don't think that's the issue that was raised by my colleague or by the General himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I did raise the issue of relevance. Really, what I was submitting - and I wanted to make it extremely short and it's now taken a long time - was that this was a step too far. And I appreciate the Trial Chamber, again, to monitor this cross-examination, and in particular I appreciate the ruling has already been made, but this document, if one compares it to what has been put hitherto, is, we submit, far too far along the road, and my learned friend shouldn't be allowed to put this sort of material to this witness in this context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I've read Mr. Josse's previous argument, he indicated that he felt that it was prejudicial which is a different question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Actually --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- a different question than whether it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What he said is the following: "I repeat my objection," and to me that means he's repeating all the arguments brought forward before which we dealt with. "This is nothing but veiled, or perhaps veiled is the wrong word. This is nothing but prejudice." This is all we have because then we had --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of prejudice, I would only respond that it is clearly not unduly prejudicial. Any evidence that the Prosecution puts in against an accused in a case is necessarily prejudicial because it proves a position contrary to the position of the Defence. The issue in terms of its admissibility or the propriety we wish to regard the document is whether it's unduly prejudicial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- and I think in light of the circumstances that have been appraised, in light of the testimony of the expert witness, and the questions put to him by Mr. Krgovic concerning the role of General Gvero, in terms of -- in terms of linking him or not linking him with Directive 7 and the specific terms related to morale and psychological support contained in that document, that this document responds specifically to that issue insofar as it concerns the presentation of information, information which undoubtedly will reach the Muslim community --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- to which it is targeted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Because the witness is also following what has been said. Incidentally, on page 52, line 3, the transcript needs to show that the speaker is accused Gvero, okay? All right. Let's me consult with my colleagues, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So our position isn't much changed from how we explained it before in the sense that we consider the question -- questions put as rising out of the previous questions and report of the witness and not being unduly prejudicial. At the same time, we do feel duty-bound to point out that the nature of this document and suggest to you that you should be in a position to make an assessment how much weight or otherwise it can be given, being what it is, and proceed with your next questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I am not sure if I got an answer to the question I put to him last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I may, General, the document that I -- well, that I read to you, the New York Times article describing what General Gvero was doing and saying, is that consistent with the role of an assistant commander for religious -- morale, religious, and legal affairs as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could the text be scrolled up a little on the screen? Thank you. I will provide a very precise answer as to how I see this article, and I'm going to give my comments on it. My position here is unfavourable because I have just been read out an excerpt from the article which does not lend itself to any deeper analysis, but I can provide comments because I am familiar with the context. Judging by the article, it was published on the 23rd of May, 1993, and it was downloaded from the internet. 23rd of May, 1993, is characterized by the lies about the demilitarisation of Srebrenica, and I perceive this article as an offensive and propaganda war against Republika Srpska because there is nothing else to it. I don't know about the credibility of the article. And as for what has been said about what General Gvero might have said, he may have, but as far as I could see from the document, I never saw or read such a position coming from him in any of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 4154, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is probably something you are more familiar with. It is a document from the command of the Drina Corps. It's dated 8 July 1995, and it's directed to the Main Staff to assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs. It's entitled "Correctness of Informing the Public About Carrying Out of Combat Operations," and it reads in the middle [indiscernible] proposal. And it says: "General, sir, we are increasingly reaching the conclusion that the events connected to Srebrenica and around Srebrenica deserve propaganda coverage of the highest possible level. So we suggest to you to more immediately engage the press centre of the Main Staff of VRS, and in particular the radio stations in Milici and Bratunac are supposed to be under the jurisdiction of the Main Staff VRS press centre. "The Muslim population in the Srebrenica enclave is attentively following both of the above-mentioned radio stations, which is a good opportunity to, from our side, work on this enclave by the media. "We ask that this proposal begin to be realised as soon as possible." First, have you seen this document before, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Having read the document or having had it read to you, doesn't this describe an appropriate function of the organ over which General Gvero has, well, control?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you read this document carefully, and I've just had the occasion to read it carefully, indeed, then you can see that this is an entirely different document. This is a document in which General Milenko Zivanovic expresses his wish for the radio stations, both civilian and military, to be placed under military authorities. They should have been under the jurisdiction of the press centre of the Army of Republika Srpska. I find this document as unusual as the previous one, and that's all I can say. And also I can see that he wants the activities of the army to extend beyond the scope of the authorities of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of a statement that was made by General Gvero on 10 July 1995, concerning the events surrounding Srebrenica? It's a statement that was admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is P02753.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you would like, I can put it on the screen and you can take a look at the page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why don't you show it to him straight away?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I please have that in e-court? Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have the next one, please? I am not sure that I have ever seen this statement or read it, and now that I have, there is nothing in it that I should have incorporated into my expert report that I submitted in due time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you aware that this statement was picked up and broadcasted by SRT on 10 July?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is the fact that the statement was made on 10 July and in fact broadcasted on 10 July consistent with what we saw on the document that I presented with you earlier, 65 ter 4154, pointing out that the Muslims were attentively paying -- attentively following the radio stations, which would suggest they could be reached by other media? Isn't that consistent?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Comment, we would suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's a comment that could be made in due course by the Prosecution. The witness can't really answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me -- do you wish to comment, Mr. Vanderpuye, or shall we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think he's perfectly capable of responding to that, Mr. President. He is an expert in this field. He's an expert in the organisation, function of the Main Staff of the VRS, and this is the conduct of one of the people who he necessarily had to evaluate in order to prepare his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you understood the question, General, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... answer it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am in a position to answer, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the previous document, one could see that General Zivanovic proposed for the radio stations to become part of the military. I don't have any proof that this proposal was ever accepted and that the radio station indeed became part of the army and were under its jurisdiction. And now I've been faced with a text, and the question is whether it is in agreement with the previous document. I can't say that it is, because the previous document was about the proposal for the radio stations to be placed under the jurisdiction of the army and to be a part of it. These are two separate things. I am an expert on organisation, indeed, and one part of the organisation in the sphere that we are discussing at the moment stops here. This is now a professional and expert analysis of the activity that is a consequence of the established organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Perhaps my question was a little inartful, because what I am referring to is the part in the document, the 8th July document, where Zivanovic says, very clearly: "This is a good opportunity to, from our side, work this enclave by the media." And what I am asking you about is in relation to the statement that you just read, whether or not that statement is consistent with that request?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect, I can't establish that relationship. In order for me to establish that relationship irrespective of your attempts, we would have to analyse more than just these two documents, and we would have to analyse the authorities of the two generals that are mentioned in the two documents. On the one hand, we have the proposal by General Zivanovic, commander, and the second thing is the authorities of General Gvero which is defined by his position and role in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me just show you how this came out as it was broadcasted, if I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's 65 ter 4155.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why? Where does this take matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you wish to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I will if you would like me to. The reason why it is relevant is because it shows precisely what this statement is, precisely how it was intended to be communicated to the Muslims side which is an information aspect of the function of the administration or the sector for morale, religious, and legal affairs. That is entirely within the purview of this witness's expertise, and it is, A, proof of the statement itself, and it's also proof of the manner in which it was intended to be communicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We say it's well outside his expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, we don't think it is necessary to proceed with your question or with what you intended to do with showing us the video or showing it to the witness. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, as part of your testimony I believe you said, as far as you were aware, contact with international officials and UNPROFOR in particular was strictly regulated. And in fact, you indicated at page 30, 032 -- 30032 of the transcript of your testimony, that only Mladic and Milovanovic had the competence and authorisation. So only the two of them were authorised to deal with UNPROFOR. Do you remember giving that statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely remember, but this sentence has been taken out of the context and my comment would be pointless. Whatever was done with UNPROFOR in the contacts that General Mladic and Milovanovic had along the line of command would be handed down to the units, and then their own respective levels, the units had their own contacts involving controls, conversations, exchanges of information, and many other things. Thus, General Mladic and Milovanovic were at the top of the system which regulated all the contacts with UNPROFOR and that was their exclusive function. And then along the line of command, they would pass down the contacts, and these contacts would be inconsistent with the situation that was on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I am not going to read you back your testimony because it's in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 41 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- 52, please in e-court. And I understand that we don't have a translation of this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you please read this into the record.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document was issued by the Main Staff of the Army Republika Srpska. It's number is 09/21-534. The date is 1 December 1994. The addressee is the Drina Corps. The document is in reference to the Main Staff document number 09/21-526. The text of the document reads: "We hereby inform you that we have approved the passage of the UNPROFOR convoy from the strength of the Dutch Battalion and to travel on the 1st of December, 1994, from Srebrenica to B Koviljacu," which probably stands for Banja Koviljacu. "Please carry out the control and enable unhindered movement." And it says below that: "The assistant commander, General Lieutenant -- Lieutenant-General Milan Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is, in effect, a notification, as you call it, or an instruction to the Drina Corps in respect of a convoy related to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document, unambiguously, says that the assistant commander Lieutenant-General Milan Gvero informs the Drina Corps what to do in respect of the fact that somebody authorised somebody with powers to do so had issued a certain decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And is there anything in the document in and of itself that suggests to you that the somebody who was authorised with respect to this convoy wasn't General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two important elements point to that fact. First of all, you can see that the system is well established and it is well known who informs whom. That's why you have this certain text "Hereby we inform you ..." and then the body of the text which contains instructions as to what to do. Second of all, it wouldn't be a common practice for General Gvero to address themselves by their second name in a polite way. One can tell that he informs somebody else and conveys somebody else's message by sheer form of address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We will have the break now, and we will resume at 6.25. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. McCloskey has understandably asked that I provide some information about where we are up to and what progress is being made. The bad news is that the Gvero expert is still in hospital in Belgrade. We understand that he's going to be discharged from there tomorrow, and were we to call him, we believe that he could be ready to start on Monday morning. So far as that decision is concerned, we are confident that we will make it during the course of tomorrow and be able to relay it to the Trial Chamber perhaps towards the end of tomorrow's sitting. The good news is - and this is really over to my learned friends from the Prosecution - is it seems to me that the Prosecution have some way to go with the present witness, and therefore, were we to call our expert, the time lost might be very small indeed. I would have thought they were going to be most of tomorrow, perhaps even into Thursday. Of course, we don't know how long the re-examination is going to take. I simply make those observations for timetabling purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't understand why we can't have a decision on this. Perhaps in the spirit of compromise we can have a decision first thing in the morning. I mean, whether you are going to call an expert? I mean, we have been doing this for a long time. You've heard a lot of this expert. You've heard the guts of what the Prosecution is going to say about him. Can't we have this by tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. On the other hand, perhaps one should not underestimate the difficulties one can encounter in trying to discuss something with someone who is lying on a bed in a hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's not really the issue, Your Honour. The issue - although I'm grateful for that - is when the Prosecution have finished asking this witness about our client, then we will be a position to make a final decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I was only trying to help, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Your Honour. And excuse me for being so robust, and I hope -- I hope I wasn't impolite, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even if you were, I'm used to it. So -- yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are having these discussions and we know what they are doing, and they know what our concern is. They have seen the rest of Mr. Vanderpuye's list. We are almost out of gas on this subject. So I think it's fair to -- to have the decision now, frankly. I think I may be time for a Court order. But tomorrow at the very least, tomorrow morning, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Anything else? Nothing. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we understand you both, of course, and we do appreciate your problems and concerns. We don't want to sound Solomonic, but I think we are going to impose splitting the difference, and therefore we are calling upon you to come back with a definitive position, an answer, Mr. Josse, before noon tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, before we bring in the witness, how much longer do you think you have, Mr. Vanderpuye, so that we can calculate better our scheduling.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I -- certainly until the end of today. And to tomorrow I would say at least one session, and I suspect it will be a second session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And you, Madam Fauveau, as things stand, I take it you would have a re-direct? What's your estimate?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think not more than 15 minutes for the moment, but I -- it might last up until an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let's bring the witness in, continue and finish at 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry for keeping you waiting, General. Mr. Vanderpuye will continue with his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could have 65 ter 4153, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is another document, and I'm afraid that the translation is not completed yet, but you can see from the top left-hand corner that this is a Main Staff -- it says Main Staff Republika Srpska. It has a document number of 09/23-321, and is dated 8 December 1994. And you can see that it's addressed to the Drina Corps. If you could just read the text of this document into the record, please, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We hereby inform you that we agree to implement the authorisation for the coordinating body for the HP," I assume it's humanitarian assistance, that's my comment, "RS number 786-MSF-112, dated the 6th of December 1994." "On the 10th of December, 1994, the MSF team shall move along the following axis: Belgrade, Zvornik, Bratunac, Srebrenica, and back. Individuals concerned: Goran Bakic, identity card, Driver, Frederique [phoen] C-h-a-p-u-i-s," if that's correct. "Passport number such and such, vehicle Toyota jeep, BG033 RP. Carry out a check-up and ensure that movement is unhindered. Assistant commander, Lieutenant-Colonel -- General Lieutenant-Colonel Milan Gvero."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that, General. Now, this document similar to the last document shows an approval for an NGO, Medecins Sans Frontieres, that is being passed down to the Drina Corps through General Gvero. Is that fair to say? And it's approval for a convoy.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not an approval for a convoy. It's information, an information according to which the coordinating body from the Republika Srpska that is responsible for humanitarian aid probably sent a document to the relevant body in the Main Staff of the VRS, and that body in the Main Staff of the VRS agreed to have this carried out and the axis was established, et cetera. So this is information according to which authorisation has been provided for this act.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In respect of this act, as you call it, why would it be necessary for the Main Staff to agree with a decision that's already been made?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire system in Republika Srpska functioned in the following way. There was always the possibility for the Main Staff could make an assessment in military terms to see whether there were any problems; and if there were any problems, it would intervene with the coordinating body. In this specific case, the assessment was that there were no problems, and as a result, this mission was authorised. In fact, this authorisation simply means that the army didn't see that there were any obstacles to the implementation of this plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, why would that be necessary to communicate that to a subordinate unit such as the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not necessary, but it's correct to say that they are informing them that they agree with this. It's not necessary, but it doesn't hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Aside from the fact that it doesn't hurt, can you explain militarily why it's there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information note exists because one can see that this assistant, this team, this vehicle have to pass through the positions of the VRS, and the VRS is responsible for anything that is located in their zone or anything passing through their zone. They have to ensure that everything runs smoothly. This doesn't mean that if the Main Staff isn't in agreement -- the Main Staff of the VRS isn't in agreement with providing authorisation that this decision would be final. That doesn't follow. They could say that they don't agree, but in that case the supreme commander would probably issue an order according to which the convoy should be allowed to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I want to know, General, is why wouldn't it be simply sufficient to advise the Drina Corps that the convoy is coming, has already been approved and is coming? Why wouldn't that be sufficient? Why is it necessary to tell the Drina Corps that the Main Staff agrees, from a military standpoint?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we both agree that can be seen in the previous answer. We would both regulate matters in the following way: We would say we agree that the convoy should pass through and that's it. But matters have been dealt with differently here and I don't think that that poses a particular problem, and I don't think that any problems were created. It wasn't necessary to regulate matters in this way, but doing so does no harm either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As far as you're aware of the issuance of this kind of a notification, this statement of agreement, however you want to put it, is it appropriate for a person in General Gvero's position to be sending this type of information on to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As information for his subordinates, it's his duty to inform his subordinates as to what his superior has decided. He relays -- he is responsible for relaying this information. He probably literally transmitted this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does that particular function fall within General Gvero's position by establishment as the assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs? Does the fact that he's sending apparent approvals of convoys to the Drina Corps fall within the functions that would normally be ascribed to him given his position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am being told by the gentleman to my left that the document doesn't actually refer to a convoy. Of course, I don't know that because I don't understand it and there is no translation. Perhaps we could clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Perhaps you can do that, Mr. Vanderpuye. We are not in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe I could clarify it through the witness, with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How do you understand this document, General? What do you understand it to be?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this at the outset. I'll repeat what I said. This is a note informing the subordinate unit as to what has been decided. As far as I could see what the responsibilities of the organisational units were, as far as I could see what responsibilities they had with regard to humanitarian organisations, well, I can't see that this is his responsibility; but as for the duty to relay the order issued to him by the commander, well, there is such a duty and it has to be fulfilled in spite of the fact that this is not his sphere of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, for that. I hope that satisfies my colleague, but my follow-up question is: Understanding that it's a duty that has to be fulfilled, why should it have been General Gvero to fulfill it, given your understanding of the Main Staff and the way the Main Staff works?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can assume that this was so because that's what the commander had decided, and this information could have been relayed by any assistant commander if the commander so decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So an assistant commander can do pretty much anything as long as he has the authorisation of his superior, the commander; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're a lawyer, but no, far from it. An assistant commander couldn't do whatever he wanted to do. An assistant commander has clearly defined duties. In the course of my testimony, I have mentioned where these duties set out and this is the field of activities that such a commander is involved in. In addition, an assistant commander can also deal with other tasks assigned to him by the commander if it's possible for him to carry out the task in question and if it's not necessary to be involved in other activities to carry out the task. It's quite obvious that in order to inform troops all you need to know is whom you have to inform and you have to know what they have to be informed of, and each and every assistant commander has been trained to act in this manner and is competent to do so if his commander issues him such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know, given your examination of many documents, whether or not General Gvero was authorised to maintain contacts with international organisations, NGOs, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We have not objected hitherto, but this line undoubtedly arises purely from the words that Mr. Vanderpuye quoted earlier, which were really words that the witness mentioned in passing in his examination-in-chief. Significantly, this was not an area that we dealt with at all in our cross-examination. They were the words that -- if I could have a moment. At 30032 -- and it might be worth the Trial Chamber looking at them and deciding whether this line should be permitted, but the essential difference is this was not cross-examined upon at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do, but regrettably I would like the witness to take his headphones off because I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. General, could you take your headphones off, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I -- this particular issue was specifically dealt with on cross-examination because it arises precisely out of the language of Directive 7 insofar as it concerns morale and psychological support. It arises directly out of that language. The -- under 6.1 it says: "Externally, a more aggressive propaganda and information presence should be maintained aimed at gaining allies, deepening discord in the coalition, unmasking the biased and hostile activities of certain individuals in parts of UNPROFOR, in some humanitarian organisations, and undermining the enemies fighting morale. This is to be achieved through a planned and organised information and propaganda activities coordinated from the state level." This specific language was challenged by the Defence in order to distance General Gvero from potentially attributing to its creation. That was the whole purpose of Mr. Krgovic's cross-examination of this witness. When the witness responded he agreed, and he said that that language was far removed from what would normally be expected in effect - I'm paraphrasing at this point because I don't have it in front of me - in effect was far removed from the responsibilities that General Gvero would have as the assistant of moral -- assistant commander for morale, legal -- morale affairs. What this is pointing at is what the extent is or the nature of General Gvero's responsibilities are insofar as they relate to the language in the document that the Defence specifically challenged. They are saying he couldn't have contributed to it because it doesn't sound like it came from him and it's not within the scope of his authorities. And what I am demonstrating -- trying to demonstrate through my cross is that that's not the case, simple and plain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. General, the question that Mr. Vanderpuye put to you and which was objected to and on which we have heard some submissions, was the following: "Do you know, given your examination of many documents, whether or not General Gvero was authorised to maintain contacts with international organisations, NGOs, et cetera?" If you have come across documents or in the course of your research obtained information which enables you to answer this question, then please go ahead and answer it. Otherwise, we will proceed to the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can provide you with the following answer: Cooperation with UNPROFOR hadn't been systematically regulated. It was an ongoing process when it came to organisation and responsibilities. Milovanovic, Manojlo's statement and other documents show that contact with UNPROFOR was dealt with at the highest level of the army and that meant through Generals Milovanovic and Mladic. In certain documents I saw that on the basis of their decision they specifically authorised certain officers in the rear to have contact or to become involved in other activities. Since I wasn't really involved in investigating the responsibilities and sphere of activities of General Gvero, as to whether he had an order to cooperate in specific cases, well, I could not say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I am afraid we have to leave it at that for today. We will resume tomorrow at 2.15. I am confident that we will finish with your testimony tomorrow, hopefully. So that's all. Thank you all, and we stand adjourned.
